scripts.opening:opening:
[hushed, ominous] The Great Chicago Fire.

Sunday night, 8 October 1871, at the end of a dry summer. Since the 3rd of July only two and a half inches of rain have fallen on Chicago, and the West Side is built of wood. A strong wind is blowing from the south-west. [short pause] The firemen are worn out: last night they fought another fire by the river, and worked on into this afternoon.

Twelve stops, hour by hour, from a cow barn on the West Side, over two rivers, to the far end of the North Side, with the night and then the day as they were. Long rides go Instantly; every place keeps its stop.

[short pause] It begins in a barn on DeKoven Street, at about nine o'clock.
scripts.stop:oleary-barn: [quietly] Sunday 8 October 1871, about nine at night, on DeKoven Street. Behind the cottage at No. 137 stands the barn of Patrick and Catherine O'Leary, who keep cows and sell the milk to the neighbours. The loft "had recently been filled with hay". [short pause] [wryly] According to legend, Mrs. O'Leary was milking when her cow kicked over a lamp. The inquiry found the O'Learys in bed, and "no proof that any person had been in the barn after nightfall that evening." [short pause] Daniel Sullivan, a drayman across the street, saw the flames; "he has a wooden leg", and he ran anyway. He got out a calf: "The hair on its back was on fire". William Lee, two doors along, runs to the drug store for the alarm key and is refused it. [short pause] "The clock struck nine." [long pause] [low] Across the river, in the Court House tower, the watchman has not yet seen the light.
scripts.stop:st-pauls: [urgent] Ninety minutes later. Half past ten, Clinton and Mather Streets. [grimly] The alarm came late, and wrong. At 9:28 Mathias Schaffer, the watchman in the Court House tower, read the light through his spy-glass and called Box 342, "nearly a mile from the fire". [short pause] One engine, the Little Giant, fought it: "For more than thirty minutes this engine battled alone." Then the gale took the fire over the firemen's heads. [short pause] Richard Riley, a railroad contractor up on a lumber pile, saw "A large mass of fire" go "whirling through the air for more than three blocks" onto the cupola of this church, St. Paul's. The church is down. [short pause] Behind it William B. Bateham's mills, with a thousand cords of kindling wood in the yard, are going too. [short pause] Bateham, a member of the city council, turns away: "The materials from this mill will fire the South Side, and nothing can prevent it now."
scripts.stop:parmelee: [tense] One hour later. Half past eleven, Jackson and Franklin Streets, across the South Branch of the river. Since half past nine brands have been falling on this side, and now one has caught. [short pause] This is the new stable of the Parmelee Omnibus and Stage Company, "the finest of its kind in the country", built for $80,000 and to have been "occupied for the first time on Wednesday". [short pause] At the stable the fire "swept down upon them with such rapidity and terrific force as to compel them to flee for their lives." By midnight the gas works on Adams Street are burning, and the shanties of Conley's Patch beside them. [short pause] Beyond lie the stone and marble blocks of LaSalle Street, a double row of "fire-proof" buildings. [short pause] One writer asked: "Would these succumb to the shower of brands and the triple-heated furnace which had been thrown about them?"
scripts.stop:court-house: [urgent] Two hours later. Half past one on Monday morning, the Court House square, in the heart of the city. Mathias Schaffer, the watchman whose alarm sent the engines astray, is still in the tower. [short pause] Since ten o'clock sparks have been falling on the roof; it has caught "five or six times", and he has put it out with two Babcock fire-extinguishers. [short pause] In the basement the mayor, Roswell B. Mason, has been giving orders since midnight: gunpowder to blow up buildings, and the jail emptied. [short pause] Captain Hickey has had the cells unlocked, and the prisoners "rushed into the street", where a passing truck of ready-made clothing is emptied in an instant; the men charged with murder go out in handcuffs. [short pause] Now the tower is alight. Schaffer and his relief, Dennis Denene, set the great bell ringing, and run for the stairs. It weighs 10,849 pounds, [low] and it is still ringing.
scripts.stop:sherman-house: [dramatic] 35 minutes later. Five past two, at the corner of Clark and Randolph. Behind you the Court House bell comes "crashing and clanging down", and Mayor Mason, who stayed until it fell, comes out to find LaSalle Street "like a furnace, all fire". [short pause] Across Clark Street is the Sherman House, seven stories, with more than three hundred guests. Hours ago men were tearing down its awnings to save it. A writer for the Post watched it: "for nearly an hour the house held good. [short pause] Suddenly, a spirit of flame came from a window in the third story on the southern face". Only the night clerk and an assistant are left to wake every room, and five ladies are sick in bed. [short pause] North of the hotel lies the main river, the last line between the fire and the North Side. [short pause] [low] The wind is already carrying it over.
scripts.stop:crosbys: [wistful] Fifteen minutes later. Twenty past two, Washington Street between Dearborn and State. From the Court House the fire has turned east, This is Crosby's Opera House, opened in 1865, with seats for 2,500. All summer it was closed while $80,000 went on new ornament, upholstery and frescoes. [short pause] It was to open again tomorrow night, Monday, with Theodore Thomas and his orchestra, and tonight, "only an hour or two before the fire, it was lit up for the first time, that its effects might be seen by gaslight." [short pause] [grimly] Now the roof catches. "In almost the time it takes to write these lines," wrote James Sheahan and George Upton, two Chicago newspapermen, the handsomest auditorium in the country is gone. The St. James Hotel next door, which "had two or three times before stood the test of fire", falls with it. [short pause] And on the far side of the main river, the North Side has caught.
scripts.stop:north-side: [urgent] Ten minutes later. Half past two, north of the main river, where the State Street viaduct comes down at Kinzie Street. [grimly] The river did not stop it. [short pause] "About the time that the Sherman House was ablaze", the wind carried the fire over the water, and it "broke out just north of the bridge, at State street." Now Wright's stable on this corner is burning. [short pause] An hour ago Judge Lambert Tree crossed the bridge when it "was then burning in spots". Mayor Mason and his son, cut off on the South Side, are coming over by the Wells Street bridge to get round the fire, and will find it here ahead of them. [short pause] North of this corner most people are asleep; many will wake to find themselves "surrounded by fire." [long pause] Half a mile away on the lake shore stands the one building that pumps the water for the whole city.
scripts.stop:water-works: [tense] Fifty minutes later. Twenty past three, Chicago Avenue at the lake shore. [short pause] Here are the Water Works: the engine house, and a hundred and fifty feet west of it the Water Tower, a stone tower round an iron column 130 feet high, up which the pumps force the water for the whole city. [short pause] The engineer, Frank Trautman, has his engines running at thirty million gallons a day. D. W. Fuller, standing by, sees "a fire-brand, apparently twelve feet in length," come whirling toward the tower and strike the corner of the engine house. "In an instant, the roof was aflame." [short pause] The roof is wood. Fuller looks at his watch: "exactly twenty minutes past three." A few minutes before four the men are driven out. [short pause] [low] The tower will stand; the engines will stop. From now on the firemen can fight only where they can draw water from the river.
scripts.stop:tribune: [measured] Four hours later. Half past seven on Monday morning, Dearborn and Madison Streets, in daylight. On this corner stands the Tribune building, which its owners call fireproof. At daybreak William Bross, a former lieutenant governor of Illinois and one of the paper's owners, rode here and "found everything safe". [short pause] When fire crept under the sidewalk into the barber's shop in the basement, Bross put it out with his partners, Joseph Medill, one of the chief stockholders, and Horace White, the editor, "with water and one of Babcock's fire-extinguishers." [short pause] The forms went down to the presses for the morning's paper. [short pause] [grimly] Then the fire came back from the south, past the great Palmer House, to McVicker's Theatre across a narrow alley. "The iron shutters on the alley side, bent by the fire, sprung out of place". The Tribune goes, and with the Water Works gone there is nothing to stop what comes next.
scripts.stop:state-street: [measured] Thirty minutes later. Eight o'clock, State Street at Washington. This store of white Massachusetts marble belongs to Potter Palmer, who built the Palmer House hotel a few blocks south. He rents it to Field, Leiter and Co., dry goods importers, for $52,000 a year. [short pause] At first light their own men were "showering that massive pile of pure marble and iron with water from their own pumping engines." [short pause] Now the streams "had ceased to run", because the Water Works are gone, and men are carrying goods out of the lower floor into wagons. The fire comes at it "from the north and eastwardly in the rear, and it soon yielded." Down State Street the Palmer House is already a ruin. On the North Side the fire has been running since half past two, and it has not stopped.
scripts.stop:ogden-house: [quietly] Four hours later. Midday on Monday, on the North Side, before the house of Mahlon D. Ogden, brother of William B. Ogden, Chicago's first mayor. [wonder] It is made of wood, and it is standing. [short pause] In front of it lies Washington Park, which filled in the night with fugitives and their furniture, until the fire came through and burned "the accumulated furniture of fifty families." [short pause] Men inside tore up the carpets, spread them over the walls and kept them wet, and when the hydrant failed, "Several barrels of cider were used to saturate the carpets". Around it now is "nothing but this solitary building in an area of 2,600 acres." [short pause] A mile north the fire is nearing St. Michael's, the great brick German church, whose steeple it will burn. Ahead of the fire, the people of the North Side are running for the lake and the old cemetery.
scripts.stop:old-cemetery: [hushed] Six hours later. Nightfall on Monday, the old City Cemetery at the south end of Lincoln Park. Most of its dead were moved years ago, leaving "some old headstones scattered about" among the grass and the small oaks. [short pause] "By nightfall on Monday there could not have been less than thirty thousand men, women, and children, huddled within this ghostly inclosure." They carried in beds, chairs and bundles, and many have watched them "burn up before their eyes." [short pause] South along the lake shore, "Along the beach were judges, merchants, doctors, workingmen, women and children", and "Ladies were seen moving their chairs into the water, and sitting on the top of the backs". Thousands more have gone west to the open prairie. [short pause] Here they are "blinded by smoke, weakened by hunger, and choking with thirst", [softly] and nobody can say where the fire will stop.
scripts.ending:the-rain: [slowly] Monday night, 9 October 1871. [short pause] At about half past ten the fire reaches the north end of Lincoln Park and burns the house of Dr. John H. Foster on Fullerton Avenue, "just twenty-five hours from the commencement of the fire, and about four miles distant from the place of its origin." [short pause] There it "spent itself". [long pause] [relieved] Then "About eleven o'clock Monday night, the sky, as if in remorse at what the fiery element had done, poured down floods of rain." In the cemetery and on the prairie the people stand in it, soaked. [long pause] [somber] The count, when it was made: 2,124 acres burned, 17,450 buildings destroyed, 98,500 people homeless, and "more than 250" dead. The mayor's first proclamation pledged the city's credit "for the necessary expenses for the relief of the suffering", and ended: "It is believed the fire has spent its force and all will soon be well."
